subject: Automotive & EVs
title: The Five-Dollar Day
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: The Five-Dollar Day.

hook.text: In 1914, Ford shocked the world by doubling his workers' wages to five dollars a day.

buildup.text: Assembly line work was brutal and repetitive. Worker turnover hit 370% per year.

discovery.text: Ford realized that well-paid workers would stay—and could actually afford to buy the cars they made.

twist.text: Other industrialists called him a traitor to his class. The Wall Street Journal called it a crime.

climax.text: Turnover dropped instantly. Productivity soared. Ford's profits actually increased.

punchline.text: Paying workers more made Ford richer, not poorer.

details.summary: In 1914, Henry Ford more than doubled wages to five dollars a day, a radical move that reduced turnover, created loyal workers, and gave employees enough income to buy the cars they built.
details.whyItMatters: The five-dollar day showed that paying workers well could be good business. It reduced costly turnover and helped create the consumer middle class that drove American economic growth.
takeaways: Ford doubled the prevailing wage to five dollars per day
Annual worker turnover dropped from 370 percent to under 16 percent
Workers could now afford the Model T they assembled

faq.question: Was Ford's five-dollar day purely generous?
faq.answer: Not entirely. It was also pragmatic. The assembly line was so monotonous that turnover was catastrophic. Higher wages stabilized the workforce and reduced the enormous costs of constantly training new hires.

faq.question: Did other companies follow Ford's wage increase?
faq.answer: Many competitors were forced to raise wages to retain workers. The move helped establish the idea of a living wage in American industry, though Ford also attached morality conditions to the pay.
